title: What makes supply elastic or inelastic

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Name the determinants of PES, work through how each one shapes the seller's response, and analyse what a difference in conditions means for a market.

blocks.heading: Four influences
blocks.text: The determinants usually named are spare capacity - whether the seller has room to raise output without new equipment; the level of stocks - whether finished goods sit in a store ready to sell; the ease of switching production or finding extra inputs - whether workers, materials and machines can be brought in quickly; and the length of the period - how much time the seller has to respond.

blocks.heading: How the influences work
blocks.text: Spare capacity works on costs: a seller with an idle kiln or an idle third of a milling line can raise output using what it already pays for, so the quantity offered follows a rising price quickly - elastic supply. Stocks work on time: a seller with goods in store can meet a price rise this week, while a seller with empty stores must first produce, which delays the response. Both mechanisms fail at full capacity: kilns already firing flat out and yards already empty leave the seller able to change the price but not the quantity, which is the inelastic case.

blocks.heading: A season of mahangu
blocks.text: Time works through the season. A mahangu grower near Oshakati who sees grain dearer in January cannot offer more grain that season, since the harvest was planted months before - the grower's supply is inelastic within the season. Across seasons the same grower can plant more fields, so supply tends to become more elastic as the period lengthens. A Japanese electronics factory shows the other side of the same rule: with parts arriving weekly and lines that run extra shifts, its supply responds within weeks, and over a year it can order new machines - the period sets the ceiling on every other determinant.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Topic 2.4 built the supply curve these conditions sit behind, and topic 2.6 showed a shift moving the price. What the shift does to quantity is what this topic measured, and what the responses mean for buyers, sellers and governments is next.
